title: Pods, Deployments & Services
description: Deploy and manage applications in Kubernetes using Pods, Deployments, and Services.

data.text: In Kubernetes, you never deploy a container directly. You wrap it in a **Pod** — the smallest deployable unit. A Pod can contain one or more containers that share the same network namespace (IP address and port space) and can mount shared volumes.

data.title: A simple Pod
data.content: This Pod runs a single Nginx container.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.25
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80

data.title: Pods are ephemeral
data.text: Pods are created and destroyed dynamically. Never create Pods directly in production — use a Deployment or another workload resource instead.

terms.definition: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — one or more containers that share storage and networking.
Ensures a specified number of identical Pod replicas are running at any given time.
A stable network endpoint that forwards traffic to a dynamic set of Pods.
A label-based query used by ReplicaSets and Services to identify which Pods they manage.

data.text: A **Deployment** is a declarative way to manage a set of identical Pods. You tell the Deployment *how many* replicas you want, and Kubernetes ensures that exact number is always running. If a Pod dies, the Deployment creates a replacement. You can also perform rolling updates and rollbacks.

data.title: A Deployment with 3 replicas
data.content: This Deployment ensures three identical Nginx Pods are always running.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80

data.caption: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which in turn manage Pods.
data.definition:
graph TB
    A[Deployment]
    A --> B[ReplicaSet 1]
    A --> C[ReplicaSet 2]

cards.title: Pod
cards.description: The smallest deployable unit, running one or more containers.

cards.title: Deployment
cards.description: A higher-level controller that manages ReplicaSets and Pods.

data.text: Pods get their own IP addresses, but these change when Pods are recreated (e.g., during a rolling update). A **Service** provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name that always points to the current set of Pods backing it. Services also load-balance traffic across Pods.

data.title: A Service for the Nginx Deployment
data.content: This Service exposes the Nginx Pods on a stable cluster IP.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP

rows: Static port on each node's IP
Quick testing without a load balancer
Maps to an external DNS name
Expose external services inside the cluster

data.title: Service discovery
data.text: A Service creates a DNS entry named <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Pods in the same namespace can reach it by just using the service name.
You apply all these resources to a cluster using `kubectl apply -f`. Let's walk through the full process.

data.title: Deploy with kubectl
data.content: Apply the YAML, check the deployment, and verify the service is working.
data.code:
kubectl apply -f nginx-deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f nginx-service.yaml

kubectl get deployments
kubectl get pods
kubectl get svc nginx-service

data.text: To update an application, change the container image in your Deployment YAML and re-apply it. By default, Kubernetes performs a **rolling update** — it gradually replaces old Pods with new ones, ensuring no downtime. If something goes wrong, you can roll back with `kubectl rollout undo`.

data.title: Updating and rolling back
data.content: Update the image, watch the rollout, and undo if needed.
data.code:
kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deployment nginx=nginx:1.26
kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deployment
kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment

data.title: Deploy a multi-tier app
data.description: Apply Deployments and Services to a real or local Kubernetes cluster.
steps: Write a Deployment YAML for a backend API (e.g., a simple Node app).
Write a Service YAML to expose it internally.
Check that pods are running with `kubectl get pods`.
Update the image to a new version and watch the rolling update.
Roll back if the new version has issues.
data.expectedOutcome: You can see rolling updates in action and know how to roll back a deployment.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Pods are the smallest deployable unit, but always use Deployments in production.
Deployments manage replica counts, rolling updates, and self-healing.
Services provide stable networking and load balancing across Pods.
Use `kubectl apply`, `kubectl get`, and `kubectl rollout` for lifecycle operations.
data.takeaway: Deployments + Services = the core pattern for running applications on Kubernetes.
